summary: This code defines a RobotPet base class and three subclasses (RobotCat, RobotBird, RobotDog) that each speak differently depending on their type, remaining battery, and mood. The battery value is kept inside the sensible range 0-100 by a property setter.

lines.text: The initializer collects the three pieces of state that every robot pet needs: a name, a battery level, and a mood.
Assigning to self.battery here does not store the value directly; it goes through the property setter below, so even the starting value gets clamped.
The @property decorator turns the method underneath into an attribute you read as pet.battery, with no parentheses.
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore signals that outside code should leave it alone and use the property instead.
This registers the next method as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to battery, which is where the validation happens.
Any negative assignment is treated as an empty battery rather than an error, so the object can never hold an impossible reading.
The upper guard means repeated charging saturates at a full battery instead of climbing forever.
Charging is written as ordinary addition because the setter already enforces the 0-100 limits for free.
The base class provides a generic talent so that every pet answers the method, and each subclass replaces it with something specific.
This is the new feature: what a pet says now depends on its state rather than being a fixed string.
The low-battery check comes first so that an exhausted pet complains about power no matter how good its mood is.
With enough charge, mood decides between the cheerful line and the neutral one below.
Reaching the end of the method gives the default greeting, covering every mood that is not "happy".
RobotCat inherits the name, battery, mood, property, and charge behaviour, so it only has to describe what makes a cat different.

Overriding speak with the same three-branch shape means calling speak on any pet works identically while the wording changes per species — this is polymorphism, and it is what the unit tests will check.
Each new species is a small subclass, which is why adding one requires no change to the base class.
The dog follows the same pattern, giving you three types whose low-battery, happy, and neutral lines can each be asserted in a test.
